title: Forces and Newton's Second Law
learning_goal: Calculate the effects of tension, friction, normal force, gravity, centripetal force, and applied forces using free-body diagrams and Newton's Second Law.

stages.title: 1. Net force changes motion
stages.content: Newton's Second Law connects net force, mass, and acceleration. The acceleration of an object depends on the net force acting on it and its mass.

stages.title: 2. Build a free-body diagram
stages.content: A free-body diagram shows the forces acting on one object. Draw each force as an arrow pointing in the force direction. Common forces include weight, normal force, friction, tension, applied force, and centripetal force.

stages.title: 3. Worked example
stages.content: A 5 kg cart experiences a net force of 20 N to the right. Using F = ma, the acceleration is a = F/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s² to the right.

stages.title: 4. Balanced and unbalanced forces
stages.content: If opposite forces cancel, the net force is zero and there is no acceleration. If they do not cancel, add forces with direction signs to find the net force before using F = ma.

stages.title: 5. Guided practice
stages.prompt: A 10 kg box is pushed with 50 N to the right while friction exerts 20 N to the left. What is the box's acceleration?
stages.hint: Find the net force first: rightward force minus leftward friction.
stages.alternate_explanation: Imagine the force arrows on a free-body diagram. The 50 N arrow is longer than the 20 N arrow, leaving 30 N unbalanced to the right.

stages.title: 6. Mastery check
stages.content: To demonstrate mastery, draw and interpret free-body diagrams, calculate net force, apply F = ma, and analyze normal force, friction, tension, gravity, applied force, and centripetal force.

concept_cards.title: Net force is the vector sum
concept_cards.content: Newton’s second law is ΣF = ma for a constant-mass object in an inertial frame. Acceleration follows net force, not necessarily velocity or the largest individual force. Choose signs and combine forces on one object first.

concept_cards.title: Identify interactions on one object
concept_cards.content: Draw weight from Earth, the normal force from a supporting surface, friction, tension, and any applied forces that exist. Label the agent of each force. Centripetal force is the net inward component supplied by these interactions, not an extra force to add.

concept_cards.title: Normal force and tension depend on conditions
concept_cards.content: On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration and no other vertical force, N = mg. In an accelerating elevator or with angled pulls this equality need not hold. For an upward-accelerating hanging mass, T − mg = ma.

concept_cards.title: Friction has two models
concept_cards.content: Kinetic friction has magnitude approximately μ_k N and opposes sliding. Static friction adjusts up to a maximum μ_s N; it is not always equal to that maximum. Friction opposes relative slipping or its tendency, which need not be opposite the object’s motion relative to the road.

concept_cards.title: Compare force and mass
concept_cards.content: At fixed mass, twice the net force gives twice the acceleration. At fixed net force, twice the mass gives half the acceleration. A negative acceleration can either slow or speed an object depending on its velocity direction.

worked_examples.prompt: A 5 kg box has an applied horizontal force of 30 N right and friction of 10 N left. Take right as positive. Find its signed horizontal acceleration.
hint_steps: Add horizontal forces with signs first.
Divide the net force by 5 kg.
worked_examples.alternate_explanation: Choose right as positive. Net force = 30 − 10 = 20 N. Use a = F_net/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s². The sign specifies direction. Vertical forces balance in this horizontal model.
alternate_explanation_steps: Choose right as positive. Net force = 30 − 10 = 20 N. Use a = F_net/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s². The sign specifies direction. Vertical forces balance in this horizontal model.
Check which object each force acts on and whether the question asks for magnitude, direction, or a comparison.
